Intelligent fleet utilisation at Delhivery

Delhivery spent ~₹97L a month hiring vehicles it already had. I led design on a tool that made sharing the default.

₹5.58Lsaved in the first 2 weeks
+6.4%vehicle utilisation, top 10 centres
196service centres live

My role Design Manager, leading 1 designer with 1 PM and our Product Director; solution validated with Ops leaders. Timeline ~3 months.

01The problem

The business was paying for capacity it already had.

Thousands of vehicles move between Delhivery's service centres every day. Each centre runs three lines of business, and each line has its own fleet.

First MilePickups from clients into the network
CartingMovement between facilities
Last MileDeliveries out to customers

Demand isn't always predictable. When a line's own fleet fell short, Ops raised an ad-hoc request and hired an extra vehicle to keep the operation running.

₹96.9La month on ad-hoc vehicles across 3 facilities — Tauru, Bhiwandi and Faridabad
₹3.5La month in estimated savings from sharing vehicles across lines of business — at these 3 facilities alone

Why? Ops could see their own demand and capacity, but not the vehicles sitting with other lines of business — so hiring was the only move they could see.

02The reframe

From buying capacity to using the capacity we have.

Before · reactive procurement

Demand → shortage → ad-hoc hire

Every gap became a purchase, because nothing else was visible.

→
After · proactive utilisation

Demand → see capacity → share → hire only if needed

Every gap starts with what's already in the network.

Our MVP — a first wedge into a much bigger problem: give Ops a shared view of vehicle capacity, and make cross-utilisation possible before an ad-hoc request is raised. The goal wasn't to eliminate ad-hoc hiring. It was to make it the last option.

03Who it's for

The job wasn't “book a vehicle.”

Operations managers, senior managers, directors and senior directors. Their job is to make sure the operation has enough vehicles for the day's workload — which really means answering five questions.

  1. How many vehicles do I need?
  2. Which vehicles are available?
  3. Should I wait for a vehicle to return?
  4. Is another line of business already using one that could work for me?
  5. Is raising an ad-hoc request actually necessary?
04How I led it

I didn't want us designing from the PM brief alone.

I pushed the team past the initial “booking” brief to understand what ad-hoc hiring was really costing, and into the facilities to see the work first-hand.

The default approach
  1. PM brief
  2. Designer interprets the problem
  3. Design a solution
What I pushed the team to do
  1. Go to the facility
  2. Observe the actual workflow
  3. Talk to operations managers
  4. Identify real friction and workarounds
  5. Then design

The facility visits changed the problem we were solving.

We validated the concept before investing in detailed design.

A designer on my team worked with the PM to prototype the planning experience in Lovable — a low-cost way to align on the workflow and surface gaps before committing to detailed design.

Prototype→align→test→iterate→design

User testing became a design habit.

Direct access to users→Test early prototypes→Small friction surfaced→Design iterations→Repeat

05The design

Designing for better decisions, not faster booking.

  1. See capacityShow vehicles across every line of business, not just your own.
  2. Evaluate alternativesHelp Ops judge whether existing capacity can cover the demand.
  3. Act on the best optionMake sharing easier than defaulting to an ad-hoc hire.

Act on the best option.

Block an idle vehicle for another line of business in two clicks, so sharing is faster than hiring.

06Small friction, high leverage

Testing after the pilot surfaced four small frictions — each with an outsized fix.

ProblemUsers didn't know where a vehicle was

FixAdded an “In Center” indicator

ProblemRecommendations were rejected without useful feedback

FixAdded structured rejection reasons

ProblemThe interaction wasn't self-explanatory

FixAdded contextual helper text

ProblemAd-hoc remained too easy

FixAdded a check before raising ad-hoc when suitable vehicles exist

07UX improvements

UX improvements

  • Before: Fragmented planning↓One planning workspace

    Ops moved between Google Sheets for planning and a separate fleet dashboard for booking. Now availability, location, status and booking sit in one workflow.

  • Before: Reactive ad-hoc requests↓Proactive capacity planning

    Managers ordered vehicles only once capacity fell short. Now they see upcoming gaps and plan against specific time slots.

  • Before: “Order a vehicle”↓“What can I share nearby?”

    The default was “I need a vehicle → raise an ad-hoc request.” The tool now starts from vehicles already available — from procurement to utilisation.

  • Before: Individual requests↓Shared fleet utilisation

    Sharing is an explicit step in planning, not an exception, so vehicles work across facilities before new capacity is brought in.

08Results

Design changed the economics of capacity

Live across 196 centres

₹5.58LEstimated ad-hoc savingsAugust 15–30, 2026
+6.4%Vehicle utilisation across the top 10 centresMay → August, now at 103.1%

Savings are across the 196-centre rollout, which is why two weeks exceed the 3-facility estimate in section 01. Utilisation compares hours vehicles were in use with their planned hours, so above 100% means vehicles worked beyond plan instead of sitting idle.

09What I learned

What I learned as a design manager

  1. Send designers to where the work happens.

    Visiting the facilities showed us the real problem. Now my designers visit DCs regularly as part of their process.

  2. Design for the whole task, not one screen.

    We followed the Ops manager's full planning task, from spotting a need to booking a vehicle. That is how we found the small problems that mattered most.

  3. Make the right choice the easy choice.

    Ops started sharing vehicles only when sharing became easier than hiring. Putting ad-hoc hiring last made the biggest difference.

  4. Talk in business numbers.

    Starting from what ad-hoc hiring cost got Product and Ops leaders on board early, and let us measure the impact.

The 30-second version

I cut Delhivery's ad-hoc vehicle hiring by giving Ops visibility into idle capacity across lines of business — so sharing became the default.

The problem
~₹97L a month on ad-hoc vehicles across 3 facilities, while vehicles sat idle in other lines of business that Ops couldn't see.
What I did
Reframed the brief from “book a vehicle” to “use the capacity we have”, got the team into the facilities, validated with a Lovable prototype, and designed a planning tool built around seeing, comparing and sharing capacity — with ad-hoc as the last option.
The result
₹5.58L saved in the first two weeks, vehicle utilisation up 6.4% across the top 10 centres, and live in 196 service centres.
